summary:
Two criminal-law regimes apply across the Palestinian Territories, and the split between them determines what a trans visitor faces. In the West Bank, criminal law derives from the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960. Jordan's 1951 revision of its own code dropped offences covering consensual private sexual conduct, and the 1960 code carried that position forward, so no provision there criminalises consensual same-sex acts. In Gaza, the Criminal Code Ordinance No. 74 of 1936 remains the governing text: section 152(2) punishes consensual same-sex "carnal knowledge" by up to ten years' imprisonment, and section 152(1)(c) sets up to fourteen years for sodomy with a child under sixteen.

Whether the 1936 ordinance is actually in force in Gaza is disputed within the source material. The Human Dignity Trust and Human Rights Watch hold it in force, and a joint statement of 11 June 2018 citing section 152(2) was issued by Human Rights Watch with the Women's Centre for Legal Aid and Counselling and Equality Now. Amnesty International does not report same-sex acts as illegal, and the legal scholar Anis F. Kassim argues the ordinance could be read as permitting homosexuality. Human Rights Watch has separately characterised the vague "unnatural offences" concepts in that section as violating privacy and non-discrimination.

Neither code names trans identity. Trans people are drawn within Gaza's criminal law through the public-morality provisions of the 1936 ordinance rather than through any trans-specific offence, and no explicit prohibition on trans identity appears anywhere in Palestinian law.

The Palestinian Authority has legislated neither for nor against homosexuality, and it is a non-signatory to key human-rights treaties. A 2003 draft Palestinian penal code would have criminalised adult consensual same-sex conduct, carrying up to five years for male-male sodomy, and whether that draft was ever implemented is unknown. Equaldex records no broad legal protections from discrimination for LGBTIQ+ people in Palestine and no legal gender recognition provisions set out.

Enforcement practice documented in the record runs well beyond the written law. Palestinian police took action against the LGBTQ organisation al-Qaws and banned its activity, prompting condemnation from rights groups; the organisation then received a wave of hate messages that activists said posed a serious threat to the community. The record also states that gay Palestinians are often arrested and tortured, and that the Palestinian Authority's usual justification for persecuting gay people is to label them collaborators. Shaul Ganon of the Israeli-based group Aguda cites two cases, within the three years preceding his statement, in which people were tried explicitly for being homosexual, and states that since the intifada, as police began increasingly enforcing Islamic law, it has been impossible to be an open gay in the Palestinian Authority. No dates are attached to Ganon's statements in this record, and no later documented instance of an explicit homosexuality charge appears here. The record also documents periodic transphobic threats and attacks without dates or counts.

Social and family persecution makes the practical reality harsher than the formal law. A Human Rights Watch report of 11 June 2018, based on interviews with 12 Palestinian women identifying as lesbian, bisexual or queer, found widespread discrimination and abuse in public and family settings. Public acceptance is ranked 130th on the Global Acceptance Index, with very little change between 2010 and 2020.

HIV prevention and care are described as inadequate. HIV-positive queer individuals often do not receive continuous antiretroviral therapy because medication is limited and social stigma is high, and comprehensive epidemiological surveillance is lacking. Only 98 HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered in Palestine between 1988 and 2017, comprising 79 AIDS cases and 19 HIV-positive cases, with the true number considered likely far higher because taboos hinder data collection. In Gaza since October 2023, the collapse of the healthcare system together with Israeli blockades has made access to life-saving HIV medication especially difficult.

Islamist actors contest LGBTQ content in education and youth spaces. The Palestinian Mujahideen Movement and the Rightly-Guided Caliphs Assembly criticised UNRWA for promoting what they see as un-Islamic values including LGBTQ issues, and the Islamic Movement in Israel opposed Israel's conversion-therapy ban. Civil society groups protecting women and children are described as vulnerable to attack in Gaza.
tangentialFactors:
CAIRO 51's country page advances a pinkwashing critique, arguing that the occupation marginalises queer and trans Palestinians alongside everyone else and documenting what it describes as de facto oppression. The framing is the publication's own; the legal findings on that page are carried in the assessment above.

Human Rights Watch's report "Audacity of Adversity" of 16 April 2018 describes LGBT people across the Middle East and North Africa finding ways to speak out through stories, cross-border alliances and national and regional movements combating homophobia and transphobia. It supplies regional movement context rather than any Palestine-specific finding on visitor risk.

Policy in Israel, not in the Palestinian Territories, governs the asylum route used by some Palestinians who flee. Around 90 LGBT Palestinians have received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence in the territories; only in June 2022 did Israel begin issuing work permits to gay Palestinians granted asylum and to those fleeing domestic violence. Before that, some faced house arrest or deportation, and LGBTQ Palestinian asylum seekers were routinely excluded from basic healthcare programmes and shelter access available to other asylum seekers.

Raw-count and ranking sources in the inventory carry no denominators. The Global Acceptance Index position of 130th is a rank among countries, and the 98 registered HIV/AIDS cases of 1988–2017 are a raw cumulative count; neither expresses a rate, and the record itself treats the HIV figure as an undercount.
